# nano-benchmark

> Command-line utilities for benchmarking JavaScript code — ns-scale hot loops and ms-scale per-run operations — with nonparametric statistics and significance testing.

- NPM: https://npmjs.org/package/nano-benchmark
- GitHub: https://github.com/uhop/nano-bench
- Wiki: https://github.com/uhop/nano-bench/wiki
- License: BSD-3-Clause
- Runtime: Node.js (every non-EOL release), Bun, Deno; no `engines` floor pinned
- Module system: ESM only (`"type": "module"`)

## Installation

```bash
npm install nano-benchmark
```

## CLI tool: nano-bench

Benchmarks multiple functions, compares them with bootstrap confidence intervals and significance tests, outputs a styled table.

### Usage

```
nano-bench [options] <file> [methods...]
```

### Arguments

- `file` — JavaScript module to benchmark. If `"self"`, prints its own file path and exits.
- `methods...` — optional function names to benchmark; omit to run every function in the export. A single name runs as a **baseline** — its statistics are reported with no significance test (nothing to compare against in isolation).

### Options

Measurement:

- `-m, --ms <ms>` — measurement time in milliseconds per sample (default: 50). The tool auto-discovers the batch size where one call takes at least this long.
- `-i, --iterations <iterations>` — fixed iteration count per sample (overrides `--ms`, skips calibration).
- `--min-iterations <n>` — minimum iterations per sample (default: 1).
- `-s, --samples <samples>` — number of samples to collect (default: 100).
- `-p, --parallel <n>` — for asynchronous functions: each sample becomes a round of `n` calls started together, and the next round starts after all of them settle and a 5 ms window. `-s` counts rounds, so `-s 100 -p 10` records 1,000 latencies per function. Calls in one round share the load, so the significance test compares per-round medians (`significance.unit: "round-medians"`). Works with either `--order`. It measures latency with `n - 1` neighbors in flight, so it changes what is measured; don't use it to finish a run faster. A value is required; `-p` with no value was one burst of all samples before 2026-09-24. Conflicts with `--isolate`.
- `--isolate` — measure each function in its own child process (same runtime; Deno gets `run -A`). The parent calibrates once and passes `-i` to every child; each child runs `--samples` + 1 samples and the first is dropped (JIT warmup). Conflicts with `--parallel`.
- `--repeat <n>` — with `--isolate`: processes per function (default 1), started in `--order` order (interleaved rotates the first function per round). With `--verbose`, each function's per-process medians are listed under the tally. With n > 1 the significance test compares per-process medians and a line reports the fastest function in each round of processes; use it to see whether a small difference survives across processes. Measured 2026-09-24 on `bench/bench-substrings.js`: `using index` varied under 1% between processes once its input was flat, while in-process it had measured 20% faster beside allocating variants, whose GCs flattened the shared input rope — the cross-function effect `--isolate` removes.
- `--gc <mode>` — force a garbage collection outside the timed window: `once` before sampling (per function in sequential order, once in interleaved order), `each` before every sample (before every round with `-p`); `none` (default) leaves collection to the runtime. The collector is found per runtime: an exposed `gc`, `Bun.gc`, or V8's `--expose-gc` turned on at run time (Node, Deno); a runtime without one gets a note and the flag is ignored. Isolated children get the same mode. Recorded as `params.gc` when a collector ran.
- `--order <order>` — `interleaved` (default): one sample of each function per round, rotating which goes first, so drift over the run lands on every function alike; `sequential`: each function's samples in turn (the pre-2026-09-24 order). Recorded as `params.order` (`interleaved` or `sequential`; files from before 2026-09-24 made with `-p` record `parallel`).

Statistics:

- `-a, --alpha <alpha>` — significance level for the confidence interval and tests (default: 0.05 = 95% CI).
- `-b, --bootstrap <bootstrap>` — number of bootstrap resamples for CI estimation (default: 1000).
- `--seed <seed>` — bootstrap RNG seed (32-bit integer). If omitted, a seed is generated and still recorded in the JSON, so every saved run is reproducible; pass it only to pin a specific value.
- `--correction <method>` — post-hoc multiple-comparison correction over the Kruskal-Wallis pairwise comparisons: `none`, `holm` (default), or `bonferroni`. See Statistical methods.
- `-v, --verbose` — show the significance test statistic, critical value, and per-comparison α.

Output:

- `--json <file>` — write a schema-v1 results JSON (raw samples + summaries + metadata). No stdout streaming — a normal run already prints a styled table.
- `--label <label>` — free-form run label recorded in the JSON (e.g. `before-opt`); overrides the file basename as the display name in `nano-bench-compare`.
- `-H, --host` — record `os.hostname()` in the JSON (opt-in; default absent).
- `--host-name <name>` — record a custom machine name in the JSON (overrides `--host`).
- `--histogram` — show a distribution histogram per function (sample shape).
- `--chart <type>` — histogram orientation: `columns` (default, vertical ridgeline) or `bars` (horizontal, side-by-side on a shared axis).
- `--bins <bins>` — histogram bin count (default: auto — scaled to the sample count and capped to the terminal size).
- `--no-emoji` — use ASCII fastest/slowest markers (`F`/`S`) instead of 🐇/🐢 (and `!` instead of the histogram's `⚠`), for terminals with shaky emoji-width handling.
- `-o, --observe` — emit User Timing marks at calibration and sampling phase boundaries, observable via `PerformanceObserver` or DevTools / `node --inspect` traces. Mark names follow `nano-bench/<function-name>/<phase>`. Default: off.

Misc:

- `--smoke` — run each selected function once (`n = 1`) and exit: a pre-flight that validates the module (imports, setup, throws/rejections) before a long collection run. Reports ok/failed with a rough duration per function; the exit code is non-zero if any function throws or rejects. Exits explicitly, so a module holding live handles (servers, watchers) can't hang the check. Measurement/statistics options are ignored.
- `-e, --export <name>` — name of the export to use from the file (default: `"default"`).
- `--self` — print the script's file path to stdout and exit (for Deno/Bun usage).

### Output

While measuring, a progress bar under the table shows the phase (calibrating, sampling by round or slice, bootstrapping), a percentage, and the time left; the final frame drops it. It appears only on a terminal.

A styled table with columns:

| Column | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| name | Function name |
| median | Median execution time |
| CI + / − | The median's bootstrap confidence interval, as distances from the median: how precisely the median is known; narrows as samples accumulate |
| spread + / − | The range most samples fall in (bootstrap estimates of the α/2 and 1−α/2 quantiles), as distances from the median: how noisy the runs are |
| op/s | Operations per second (1000 / median) |
| batch | Iterations per sample (batch size) |

Under the table, a `⚠ name: N of M samples were preempted …` line comes first when 10% or more of a function's samples got less than 90% of the CPU (thread CPU time from `process.threadCpuUsage()` when it is fine-grained, else `process.cpuUsage()`, chosen by probing; synchronous samples only, not with `--parallel`); it names CPU contention from another program as the cause. The counts are saved as `results[].contention` (`samples`, `preempted`, `medianRatio`), and `nano-bench-compare` and the viewer repeat the warning. Then a `⚠ name: distribution looks multimodal (dip test …)` line marks any function whose samples fail the dip test (p < 0.05, seeded with the run's seed, so `nano-bench-compare` flags the same series). A batched median then describes only the fast clump; `nano-bench-io` measures one call per run and reports p90/p99.

When two or more functions are measured, a `Significance:` line names the test, α, and (for 3+ functions) the post-hoc method and correction. For two functions an `Effect size:` line follows — Cliff's δ with a magnitude label (Romano et al. thresholds) and how often the faster wins a random pair of runs (Vargha-Delaney A12, derived from the same rank sums; both persisted into the JSON `significance` object). If the difference is significant, an N×N matrix of pairwise percentage/ratio differences follows. For three or more functions an `Effect sizes:` matrix follows the significance matrix: Cliff's δ for every pair with its magnitude label, shown whether or not the omnibus was significant, and persisted as `significance.effects` (k×k, antisymmetric, `effects[i][j]` positive when i tends to be slower than j). The fastest function is marked with 🐇 and the slowest with 🐢 (`F`/`S` under `--no-emoji`). With `--histogram`, a per-function distribution chart follows; with `--json`, a results file is written.

### How it works

1. **Find level**: auto-discovers batch size `n` where `fn(n)` takes ≥ `--ms` milliseconds.
2. **Collect samples**: runs `fn(n)` `--samples` times, collecting timing data (normalized to ms/iteration).
3. **Bootstrap**: seeded resampling estimates the median, its percentile confidence interval, and the spread of the samples.
4. **Significance test**: Mann-Whitney U (2 functions) or Kruskal-Wallis H + Conover-Iman pairwise post-hoc (3+ functions), with `--correction` controlling the post-hoc family-wise error rate.
5. **Optional outputs**: a distribution histogram (`--histogram`) and/or a schema-v1 results file (`--json`).

The run ends with an explicit `process.exit(0)` once reporting (and the `--json` write) completes, so a module holding live handles (servers, watchers) can't keep a finished run alive.

### Example

```bash
npx nano-bench bench/bench-string-concat.js
npx nano-bench -s 200 -b 2000 -a 0.01 bench/bench-string-concat.js
npx nano-bench bench/bench-string-concat.js plus template   # only these two
npx nano-bench bench/bench-string-concat.js --json base.json --label baseline
npx nano-bench bench/bench-string-concat.js --smoke         # pre-flight: each function once
```

---

## CLI tool: nano-bench-io

Benchmarks slow (ms-scale and up) functions one call per run — no batching — so the run-to-run distribution and its tail stay visible. Same module format as nano-bench; each selected function is called with `n = 1` and awaited. Reports the bootstrap median CI plus p90/p99 tail percentiles, files modified-z outlier notes, and reuses nano-bench's significance tests, histograms, JSON export, and `--smoke`.

### Usage

```
nano-bench-io [options] <file> [methods...]
```

### Run policy

- Default: keep running while runs < `--min-runs` (default: 10; 30 with `--stable`) *or* elapsed < `--budget <ms>` (default: 5000), per function; capped by `--max-runs` (default: 1000).
- `-r, --runs <runs>` — exact run count (overrides the stop policy).
- `--settle <pct>` — stop on the question instead of on precision: run until every pair of functions is settled against ±pct%, at two checks in a row (every 10 rounds from `--min-runs`, which defaults to 30; capped by `--max-runs`). A pair is settled when the bootstrap percentile CI (at `--alpha`, per pair, not corrected for the number of pairs) of the log ratio of its medians lies wholly beyond ±log(1 + pct/100), a difference of at least pct%, or wholly inside it, no difference that big. Needs two or more functions and interleaved order; conflicts with `--runs`, `--stable`, and `--isolate`. A `Settle:` block lists each pair's verdict with its ratio CI, and a note names the pairs still open when `--max-runs` stopped the run. Recorded as `params.settle`, `params.settleChecks: 2`, and a top-level `settle` block: `{threshold, reason: 'settled' | 'max-runs', rounds, pairs: [{a, b, state, ratioLo, ratioHi}]}`, where `state` is `faster` (a is faster than b by at least the threshold), `slower`, `equivalent`, or `unsettled`.
- `--gc <mode>` — `once` after warmup, `each` before every run (after `prepare()`, before the timed call and the metrics reading); same collector lookup and `params.gc` as nano-bench. Refused with `-c`, where a collection in nano-bench-io would not reach the commands.
- `--stable <pct>` — adaptive stop: run until the bootstrap CI on the median is <= pct% of the median at **two checks in a row** (checked every 10 runs from `--min-runs`, which defaults to 30 under `--stable`; capped by `--max-runs`). Recorded as `params.stable` and `params.stableChecks: 2`. Before 2026-09-25 it stopped at the first passing check from 10 runs; a simulation over collected populations showed that under-covered the median (as low as 82.5% for a 95% CI), see `dev-docs/stable-stopping.md`.
- `--order <order>` — `interleaved` (default): each round runs every function once, rotating which goes first, so drift over a long run lands on every function alike. The stop policy then counts rounds: `--runs`, `--min-runs`, and `--max-runs` are rounds; the budget is `--budget` × the number of functions, for the whole loop; a `--stable` check passes only when every function's CI width is within the target; `--warmup N` is N discarded rounds. `sequential`: each function's runs in turn, each with its own policy (the only order before 2026-09-25). Recorded as `params.order`. With one function the two are the same.
- `--isolate` — run each function's whole stop policy in its own child process (same runtime; Deno gets `run -A`) through a hidden `--emit-runs` child mode. Children keep every run: unless `--warmup` is explicit, warmup auto-detection runs on each process's runs in the parent, and a note reports how many processes dropped runs. With `-M`, the rusage deltas come from each function's own process. Conflicts with `-c` (a command already runs in its own process).
- `--repeat <n>` — with `--isolate`: processes per function (default 1), started in `--order` order. With n > 1 the significance test compares per-process medians and a line tallies which function had the fastest median in each round of processes, as in nano-bench.
- `-w, --warmup <runs>` — discarded warmup runs per function (fills caches, JIT, connections). When omitted, warmup is auto-detected after collection (a windowed Mann-Whitney screen drops leading runs that read significantly slower than the rest, capped at 25% of the runs) and discarded with a note reporting the count; the per-series `warmupDetected` lands in the JSON. `--warmup N` pins the count, `--warmup 0` keeps everything — an explicit flag disables detection.

### Per-run hooks

The module may export `prepare()` / `teardown()` (named exports, sync or async) — awaited untimed around every run, warmup included. Use them to reset state so every run measures the same thing (drop a cache, open a fresh connection, recreate a temp file).

### Command mode

`-c, --command` treats the arguments as shell commands to benchmark instead of a module file — whole-process macro benchmarking (hyperfine's niche, with nonparametric statistics):

```bash
npx nano-bench-io -c 'node script.js' 'bun script.js'
npx nano-bench-io -c -w 2 --prepare 'sync' 'tar xf big.tar'
```

- Each command runs via the system shell; stdout/stderr are discarded (output would garble the live table and skew timing).
- `--prepare <cmd>` — a shell command run untimed before every run (the canonical cold-cache recipe).
- A run **fails** when the child exits non-zero or dies by a signal — `--smoke` reports it per command; a measured run aborts with the error.
- Series are named by the command string; the JSON records `source: {commands}` and a `bodyHash` of the command text. Everything else (stop policies, percentiles, outlier notes, significance, histograms) works exactly as in module mode.

### System metrics (`-M, --metrics`)

Opt-in per-run system metrics: printed as a second table of medians and persisted into the `--json` results (raw per-run readings, `params.metrics` naming the collector).

- **Module mode** — per-run `process.resourceUsage()` deltas, taken outside the timed window: CPU user/sys time, minor/major page faults, voluntary/involuntary context switches. Works on Node, Bun, and Deno.
- **Command mode (Linux)** — `/proc/[pid]/{io,status}` of the **command's process tree**: peak RSS (`VmHWM`, bytes; max of any single process), logical (`rchar`/`wchar`) and physical (`read_bytes`/`write_bytes`) I/O, and `syscr`/`syscw` syscall counts (summed over the tree). The wrapper shell that spawns the command is excluded — its readings never pass as the command's. Polled on an adaptive backoff — every 1 ms for the command's first 100 ms, then every 5 ms, then every 25 ms past 3 s — and the last successful poll wins, so a sliver of trailing activity can be missed (negligible for genuinely slow processes). A command living only a few ms typically yields no reading; a per-command note reports the capture count (`metrics captured in N of M runs`), and below half the runs the row is reported blank rather than as a fake median over a slow-run-biased minority. Other platforms skip command metrics with a note.
- Network-specific byte counts are not portably available without tracing; syscall counts are the proxy.

### Cluster analysis (`--clusters`)

Latency distributions are often multimodal (fast path vs slow path, cache hit vs miss) — one median then lies the same way one mean does. Every run set is gated by a Hartigan-style dip test (the statistic is bootstrap-calibrated against the uniform null with a seeded RNG, so the p-value stays honest): a multimodal distribution gets a note suggesting `--clusters`, and the flag splits the samples at the KDE density minima (Gaussian kernel, Silverman bandwidth), reporting per cluster: weight (the fast/slow split as a %), median with bootstrap CI, and its min/max bounds (separate columns). The **mode count is a labeled heuristic** — reported for confirmation, never asserted. When the dip test fires but KDE finds a single mode (heavy skew), a note says so instead. The same gate and flag exist on `nano-bench-compare` for saved runs.

### Other options

Shared with nano-bench: `-e, --export`, `-a, --alpha`, `-b, --bootstrap`, `--seed`, `--correction`, `-v, --verbose`, `--histogram` / `--chart` / `--bins`, `--no-emoji`, `--json` / `--label` / `-H, --host` / `--host-name`, `--smoke`, `--self`.

### Output

While measuring, a progress bar under the table follows the stop policy (rounds when interleaved, processes with `--isolate`): runs done out of `--runs`, the slower of `--min-runs` and `--budget` by default, or the latest CI width against the `--stable` target (reported each check by `collectMacro` as a `macro-check` event). The summary table adds `p90` / `p99` columns and a `runs` column (batch is always 1). After the table: outlier notes (modified z-score > 3.5, slow side only) distinguishing a slow *first* run (caching — consider `--warmup`) from scattered slow runs (interference from other programs), plus a coarse-tail note when a function ran fewer than 100 times (p99 lands on the few slowest runs). Significance testing and histograms work exactly as in nano-bench.

`--json` writes the same schema-v1 results file with `params.mode: "macro"`, `params.order`, per-series `reps: 1` (with `--isolate`, `warmupDetected` is an array of per-process counts), `p90` / `p99` added to the stored summary, and (with `--metrics`) the raw per-run readings — `nano-bench-compare` renders those side by side, so memory and I/O diff across runs the same way timing does.

### Example

```bash
npx nano-bench-io io-bench.js                      # at least 10 runs and 5 s per function
npx nano-bench-io io-bench.js -r 50                # exactly 50 runs
npx nano-bench-io io-bench.js --stable 5           # run until the median CI width is <= 5%
npx nano-bench-io io-bench.js -w 3 --histogram     # discard 3 warmup runs, show shapes
```

---

## CLI tool: nano-bench-compare

Reads nano-bench results JSON and renders a view/compare table — **recomputing** significance and CIs from the saved raw samples (it never benchmarks). Use it to render one saved run, or to compare a baseline against a new run (before/after) without re-measuring. When files carry per-run system metrics (recorded by `nano-bench-io --metrics`), their medians render side by side in a metrics table after the summary — memory and I/O diff across runs the same way timing does; series without metrics are simply absent from that table. Multimodal series are flagged by the dip test, and `--clusters` splits them per cluster exactly as in `nano-bench-io`.

### Usage

```
nano-bench-compare [options] <files...>
```

### Arguments

- `files...` — one or more results JSON files written by `nano-bench --json`.

### Options

- `-a, --alpha <alpha>` — significance level for the recompute (default: the first file's recorded α).
- `--correction <method>` — post-hoc correction for the recompute: `none` / `holm` / `bonferroni` (default: the first file's recorded method).
- `--pooled` — compare all series as one k-sample Kruskal-Wallis omnibus instead of pairing by name.
- `-v, --verbose` — show test statistics and critical values.
- `--histogram`, `--chart columns|bars`, `--bins <bins>` — distribution histograms (one chart per series on a shared axis).
- `--no-emoji` — ASCII `F`/`S` markers.

### Comparison modes

- **Paired by name (default)** — partition series by `name`; run one before/after test per name that appears in ≥2 of the files (2 series → Mann-Whitney; 3+ → Kruskal-Wallis within that name). Names appearing once are shown in the summary table but not tested ("not compared"). This is the headline "save a baseline, run a new version, compare" case.
- **Pooled (`--pooled`)** — throw every series into one Kruskal-Wallis omnibus + Conover-Iman post-hoc matrix. Answers "which of these k series differ from which" — but for a before/after it buries the meaningful same-name cells and lets unrelated series perturb the ranks, so it is opt-in.
- **Degrade** — with no shared name (a single file, or disjoint names), paired mode falls back to one omnibus so a single-file render still reproduces the in-run table.

### Comparability banner

The raw samples make recompute exact, but they do not make a cross-machine comparison *valid*. `nano-bench-compare` diffs the recorded environments and warns loudly above the results on any mismatch — runtime/engine version, OS/arch, CPU model/count, total memory — and on `params` (α/samples/bootstrap/correction) or per-series `bodyHash` divergence. `host` and `cpu.speedMHz` are shown as provenance but never trigger a warning. A differing `bodyHash` for a same-named pair means the code changed (the delta may be real); an identical one means any delta is environment/noise.

### Determinism

Each series' CI is reproduced exactly from its saved samples + the run's recorded `params.seed` + its series index + `params.bootstrap` (per-series `mulberry32` streams). The rank tests are deterministic regardless. So a recompute reproduces the original run's verdict and interval rather than silently re-deciding.

### Example

```bash
npx nano-bench-compare base.json                       # render one saved run
npx nano-bench-compare base.json new.json              # before/after, paired by name
npx nano-bench-compare base.json new.json --pooled     # one omnibus over all series
npx nano-bench-compare base.json new.json -a 0.01      # recompute at a different α
```

---

## CLI tool: nano-bench-view

Serves a browser viewer for nano-bench results JSON. It runs tape-six's test server (`tape-six/test-server.js`, an optional peer dependency loaded lazily) over a root folder with two plugins, so it needs no build step and no configuration. Useful when the results sit on a remote machine: start it there, forward the port over SSH (`ssh -L 3000:localhost:3000 HOST`), and open the printed URL from a local browser.

**Security:** the server is strictly a development tool. It is not hardened and not meant for general web serving: it serves every file under the root folder to anyone who can reach it, with no authentication. The user is responsible for its security; outside `localhost` they are on their own. `--host` with a non-loopback address prints a warning at startup.

### Usage

```
nano-bench-view [options] [files...]
```

### Arguments

- `files...` — optional results files inside the root folder; the printed viewer URL opens them directly (`?view=<path>` per file).

### Options

- `-r, --root <folder>` — folder to serve and search for results (default: the current folder).
- `--host <host>` — interface to listen on (default: `localhost`). Anything else exposes the unhardened server beyond this machine; see **Security**.
- `-p, --port <port>` — port (default: 3000; an occupied port is reported with a hint).
- `--show-dot-files` — include dot-files in folder listings.
- `--trace` — log every request.

### Routes

- `/` — redirects to the viewer at `/--nano-bench/web-app/`.
- `/--nano-bench/web-app/?view=a.json&view=b.json` — view one file, or compare several (paired by name, as in `nano-bench-compare`).
- `/--nano-bench/results` — JSON list of results files under the root (`path`, `size`, `mtime`, `label`, `createdAt`, `source`, `series`, `runtime`, `host`); dot-folders and `node_modules` are skipped, and a file qualifies when its first 512 bytes carry `schemaVersion: 1` and `tool: "nano-benchmark"`.
- `/--nano-bench/web-app/?run=bench/bench-x.js` — run a bench file in the browser (see **Browser runner**); optional `ms`, `samples`, and `export` query parameters.
- `/--nano-bench/benches` — JSON list of bench files under the root (`path`, `size`, `mtime`): `bench[-_.]*.js` and `*.bench.js` (`.mjs` too), skipping dot-folders and `node_modules`.
- `/--nano-bench/save?name=<name>` — `POST` a results JSON body to write it to `nano-bench-results/<name>.json` under the root. The reply is `{path}`. A name collision adds `-2`, `-3`, and so on, so no file is overwritten. Anything but schema v1 from `nano-benchmark` is refused with `400`; the body is capped at 50 MB.
- `/--nano-bench/frame?file=<url>&fn=<name>` — the benchmark iframe page, with the root's tape6 import map inlined so bench files can use bare imports.
- `/--nano-bench/meta` — `{name, version}` of the package.
- `/?list` and any folder URL without `index.html` — an HTML directory listing; JSON files get a **view** link.
- Any other path — the file under the root, served by tape-six's static handler.

Remote plugin registration (`PUT /--plugins`) is off. The viewer's own files, `src/`, and the `console-toolkit` formatters are served from wherever the package is installed, so the root can be any project.

### Viewer

- **Picker** — results on the server (select several to compare) and local files opened through a file input (read by the browser, not uploaded).
- **Files** — source, creation time, runtime, OS, CPU, and parameters per file.
- **Warnings** — the comparability banner of `nano-bench-compare` plus the dip-test multimodality flag.
- **Summary** — median, CI, spread, op/s, and batch per series, recomputed from the samples with the recorded seed; all rows share one time unit.
- **Distribution** — one histogram row per series on a shared axis, with the median line, the median's CI as a bar on top of it, and the spread shaded. Axis modes: **Auto** (logarithmic when the pooled 1st–99th percentile range spans more than 20×, else linear), **Linear**, **Log**, and **Per row** (each series on its own axis: shapes compare, positions do not). Hover a column for its range and count.
- **Significance** — the test, effect size for pairs, the pairwise matrix ("faster" or "slower", row against column), and for three or more series the Cliff's δ matrix.
- **Theme** — Auto (follows the OS), Light, or Dark; saved in `localStorage`.

### Browser runner

- **Start** — the picker lists bench files on the server (`?run=<path>`) and opens a local one through a file input (run from a blob URL, so it can't import relative files). Its bare imports still resolve through the import map.
- **Isolation** — one same-origin iframe per function, so each function gets its own global object and module instance; the iframes share the tab's thread and heap. Every page the server sends carries COOP `same-origin` and COEP `require-corp`, so the page is cross-origin isolated and `performance.now()` steps 5 µs (Chromium) or 20 µs (Firefox, WebKit) instead of 100 µs or 1 ms. The runner records `crossOriginIsolated` and the measured step and runs either way; when the page isn't isolated, it shows a warning with the step and its share of a sample, and the viewer and `nano-bench-compare` repeat it for the saved file (`isolationWarning` in `src/bench/results/series.js`). Browsers grant isolation only in a secure context (HTTPS or `localhost`); a page opened as `http://<lan-host>:3000/` is neither. The function body hash uses `crypto.subtle` when present and a bundled SHA-256 (`src/utils/sha256.js`) otherwise, so the hashes match the CLI's in every context.
- **Progress** — `<nano-bench-progress value max>` (`web-app/components/nano-bench-progress.js`), a light-DOM custom element styled by tag in `app.css`: `value` of `max` (default 1) sets the fill, and no `value` makes it indeterminate (a transform-only animation, off under reduced motion). The runner sets `max` to one step per calibration plus one per sample; loading and the statistics are indeterminate. It can be driven by hand from the console: `document.querySelector('nano-bench-progress').setAttribute('value', 0.5)`.
- **Tracing** — add `trace` to the run URL to log each progress update to the console with a timestamp, the value, and the fill's rendered box.
- **Sampling** — each function is calibrated to `ms` per sample (`findLevel`), then sampled in interleaved rounds (one sample of each function per round, starting position rotated), with a 5 ms pause between samples. The runner waits while the tab is hidden and counts those pauses. **Stop** ends the run early; at least 2 samples per function are needed to save.
- **Output** — a schema-v1 results object: `environment.runtime` is the browser (`chromium`, `edge`, `firefox`, `webkit`) with its engine. `environment.browser` holds `userAgent`, `crossOriginIsolated`, `timerResolutionMs`, `isolation`, `hiddenPauses`, and `stoppedEarly`, and `params.order` is `interleaved`. It is saved through `/--nano-bench/save` and opened in the viewer. If saving fails, it is shown locally with a download link.
- **Not measured in a browser** — CPU contention (no CPU-time clock) and process isolation.

### Example

```bash
npm install --save-dev tape-six
npx nano-bench bench.js --json runs/base.json
npx nano-bench-view runs/base.json
```

---

## CLI tools: nano-bench-playwright and nano-bench-puppeteer

Run a bench file in browsers from the command line, over the browser runner's page. Each bin starts tape-six's server with nano-bench's plugins on a free `localhost` port (so the page is cross-origin isolated), opens `/--nano-bench/web-app/?run=<file>` in each requested browser **one after another** (one at a time: parallel runs share cores and the turbo budget and bias each other), and prints each saved file through `nano-bench-compare`. The drivers are optional peer dependencies imported lazily; a missing driver prints its install command and exits 1, and a browser that fails to launch prints the command that installs it.

### Usage

```
nano-bench-playwright [options] <file>
nano-bench-puppeteer [options] <file>
```

### Options

- `-b, --browser <names>` — comma-separated browsers. Playwright: `chromium` (default), `firefox`, `webkit`. Puppeteer: `chrome` (default), `firefox`.
- `-m, --ms <ms>` — measurement time per sample (default: 50).
- `-s, --samples <samples>` — samples per function (default: 100).
- `-e, --export <name>` — the export holding the functions (default: `default`).
- `-r, --root <folder>` — the folder to serve (default: the current folder). The bench file must be inside it; bare imports resolve through the root's tape6 import map.
- `--headed` — show the browser windows.
- `--timeout <seconds>` — give up on a browser after this long (default: never).
- `-v, --verbose`, `--histogram`, `--no-emoji` — passed to `nano-bench-compare`.

### Behavior

- **Following a run:** the driver exposes `nanoBenchDriver` to the page (`page.exposeFunction`); the page calls it with `{type: 'progress', label, value, max}`, `{type: 'warning', message}`, `{type: 'error', message}`, and `{type: 'saved', path}`. Push instead of polling keeps the driver from queuing tasks on the thread the benchmark iframes share. On a terminal, progress is drawn as the CLI progress line.
- **Output:** results are saved by the page to `nano-bench-results/<bench>-<browser>.json` under the root (`-2`, `-3`, … on collision). After each browser, its file is printed by `nano-bench-compare`; at the end, the saved paths are listed.
- **Exit status:** 0 when every browser saved its results; 1 when a browser failed to launch, the run reported an error, or `--timeout` expired. Ctrl-C closes the browser and the server.
- **Engines:** Playwright's `webkit` is a WebKit build of Playwright's own, separate from Safari and Epiphany (WebKitGTK); to measure those engines, open the page in them.
- **Runtime:** the drivers run on Node.js.

### Example

```bash
npm install --save-dev tape-six playwright
npx playwright install chromium firefox
npx nano-bench-playwright bench/bench-sort.js -b chromium,firefox -s 50
```

---

## CLI tool: nano-bench-suite

Runs several bench files, each in its own process, over one or more passes, and closes with a table of which function was fastest in each file and how often that held. It replaces a shell loop such as `write-bench`'s `bench/run-all.sh`.

### Usage

```
nano-bench-suite [options] <files...> [-- <options for every run>]
```

### Options

- `<files...>` — bench files or glob patterns. Patterns are expanded with `fs.glob` (so a quoted pattern works where the shell does not expand it), sorted, and deduplicated; a pattern that matches nothing is an error.
- `--passes <n>` — passes over all the files (default: 1). Separate processes are what show that a direction survives: significance is measured within one process.
- `--io` — run `nano-bench-io` for every file instead of `nano-bench`.
- Everything after `--` is passed to every run, for example `-- -s 200 --gc each`.

### Behavior

- Each run's output streams as it would on its own, under a `----- file (pass p of N) -----` header.
- Each run writes its results to a temporary `--json` file; a parameterized file leaves one per value, and each value gets its own row.
- The closing `Suite:` table lists each file (with `[value]` for a parameter value), the function that was fastest in the most passes, and `held`: in how many passes that function was fastest with a significant difference (`—` for a file with one function).
- Exit status: 0 when every run succeeded, 1 otherwise (a failed run's rows are missing, and a line counts the failures).

### Example

```bash
npx nano-bench-suite 'bench/bench-*.js'                 # every file once
npx nano-bench-suite 'bench/bench-*.js' --passes 5      # five passes: do the directions hold?
npx nano-bench-suite --io 'bench/io-*.js' -- -r 50      # nano-bench-io, 50 runs per function
```

---

## Results JSON schema (v1)

`nano-bench --json out.json` writes this shape. The **raw per-sample arrays are the source of truth** — significance and CIs are always recomputed from them; the stored summaries are FYI only.

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "tool": "nano-benchmark",
  "toolVersion": "1.0.16",
  "createdAt": "2026-06-03T12:00:00.000Z",
  "label": "baseline",
  "source": {"file": "bench/bench-string-concat.js", "export": "default", "methods": ["plus", "template"]},
  "environment": {
    "host": "nuke",
    "runtime": {"name": "node", "version": "22.11.0", "engine": "v8 12.4"},
    "os": {"platform": "linux", "release": "7.0.0", "arch": "x64"},
    "cpu": {"model": "AMD Ryzen 9 …", "count": 16, "speedMHz": 3600},
    "totalmemMB": 64000
  },
  "params": {"ms": 50, "minIterations": 1, "samples": 100, "bootstrap": 1000, "seed": 12345, "alpha": 0.05, "correction": "holm", "parallel": false},
  "results": [
    {
      "name": "plus",
      "bodyHash": "sha256:…",
      "reps": 100000,
      "samples": [0.000123, "… ms/iteration, full precision …"],
      "summary": {"median": 0.000124, "lo": 0.000119, "hi": 0.000131, "ciLo": 0.0001236, "ciHi": 0.0001245, "mean": 0.000126, "stdDev": 0.0000044, "opsPerSec": 8064516, "ci": "bootstrap-percentile"}
    }
  ],
  "significance": {"test": "mann-whitney-u", "value": -3.42, "alpha": 0.05, "limit": -1.959, "different": true}
}
```

- `label`, `environment.host` and `params.iterations` (in place of `ms`) appear only when their flags are used; `significance` is present only when ≥2 series were measured.
- `params.seed` is always recorded (the `--seed` value or an auto-generated one), making every run reproducible.
- `summary.lo` / `summary.hi` are the spread (bootstrapped α/2 and 1−α/2 quantiles of the samples); `summary.ciLo` / `summary.ciHi` are the median's bootstrap percentile confidence interval, written since 2026-09-24. Tools recompute both from `samples`, so older files without `ciLo` / `ciHi` still render them.
- `results[].contention` (`{samples, preempted, medianRatio}`) records the per-sample CPU/elapsed check for synchronous functions; absent when no sample could be checked.
- With `-p N`: `params.parallel: N` (otherwise `false`), `samples` holds the latencies round by round (`params.samples` rounds of N), and with N > 1 `significance.unit` is `"round-medians"`; `nano-bench-compare` and the viewer test per-round medians whenever every compared series has rounds. Files from before 2026-09-24 record `parallel: true` for a single burst and are tested on their samples.
- With `--isolate` (nano-bench and nano-bench-io): `params.isolate: true`, `params.repeat`, and `results[].processSizes` (sample counts per process, in round order; `samples` is their concatenation). With `repeat` > 1, `significance.unit` is `"process-medians"`, and `nano-bench-compare` and the viewer test per-process medians whenever every compared series has more than one process.
- `results[].bodyHash` is `sha256(fn.toString())` — the per-function comparability guard. Blind spots: closures (source text doesn't capture closed-over values) and imported implementations.

---

## CLI tool: nano-watch

Continuously benchmarks a single function in streaming mode, showing live statistics and memory usage. Runs indefinitely until stopped with Ctrl+C (or until `--iterations` is reached).

### Usage

```
nano-watch [options] <file> [method]
```

### Arguments

- `file` — JavaScript module to benchmark. If `"self"`, prints its own file path and exits.
- `method` — optional method name if the export is an object of functions (same format as nano-bench).

### Options

- `-m, --ms <ms>` — measurement time in milliseconds per sample (default: 500).
- `-i, --iterations <number>` — number of iterations to run (default: Infinity).
- `-e, --export <name>` — name of the export to use from the file (default: `"default"`).
- `--self` — print the script's file path to stdout and exit.

### Output

A live-updating styled table with:

| Row | Columns |
|-----|---------|
| Stats | #, time, mean, stdDev, median, skewness, kurtosis |
| op/s | operations per second for time, mean, median |
| memory | heapUsed, heapTotal, rss |

All statistics are computed using online/streaming algorithms (constant memory):
- **StatCounter**: streaming mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis (Welford's algorithm).
- **MedianCounter**: approximate streaming median (median-of-medians).

A bounded run (`--iterations`) ends with an explicit `process.exit(0)`, so a module holding live handles can't keep a finished run alive.

### Example

```bash
npx nano-watch bench/watch-sample.js
npx nano-watch bench/bench-string-concat.js backticks
npx nano-watch -i 50 bench/watch-sample.js
```

---

## Benchmark file format

The benchmarking tools import a JavaScript module. The module should export (default or named) either:

### Object of functions (for nano-bench / nano-bench-io, or nano-watch with method argument)

```js
export default {
  variant1: n => {
    const a = 'a', b = 'b';
    for (let i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
      const x = a + '-' + b;
    }
  },
  variant2: n => {
    const a = 'a', b = 'b';
    for (let i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
      const x = `${a}-${b}`;
    }
  }
};
```

### Parameterized files (a factory export, for nano-bench / nano-bench-io)

To ask how the functions scale, export a factory that takes one parameter value and returns the object of functions, plus the values in `params`:

```js
export const params = [100, 1000, 10000];

export default size => {
  const data = Array.from({length: size}, (_, i) => i); // setup, outside the timing
  return {
    'for loop': n => {
      let sum = 0;
      for (let k = 0; k < n; ++k) for (let i = 0; i < data.length; ++i) sum += data[i];
      return sum;
    },
    reduce: n => {
      let sum = 0;
      for (let k = 0; k < n; ++k) sum += data.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
      return sum;
    }
  };
};
```

The factory runs once per value, so per-value setup stays outside the timing. The tool runs each value in its own child process (the parent spawns itself with a hidden `--param-json` flag), with every other option passed through, and each value is its own comparison block: summary, significance, histograms. A closing `Scaling:` table gives the median per call by function and value. `--params 10,100` overrides the file's `params` (numbers are parsed, anything else stays a string). With `--json out.json`, each value writes `out-<value>.json` and records `params.param`. A factory without `params` or `--params` is an error. `--isolate` works inside each value's run.

### Single function (for nano-watch without method argument)

```js
export default n => {
  const a = 'a', b = 'b';
  for (let i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    const x = a + '-' + b;
  }
};
```

### Key design principle

Each function takes `n` (iteration count) and runs the measured code in a `for` loop. This amortizes function-call overhead over `n` iterations, which is critical for micro-benchmarks where the measured code is faster than the overhead of calling a function.

The batch size `n` is either specified via `--iterations` or auto-discovered by the tool so that one call takes at least `--ms` milliseconds. `nano-bench-io` always passes `n = 1` — at ms scale one call is directly measurable and batching would erase the per-run distribution; keep the loop anyway so the same file works in every tool.

### Async functions

Benchmark functions can return a Promise (be async). The tools detect thenables and measure the time until resolution.

---

## Deno and Bun support

Use `--self` to get the script path, then run with the alternative interpreter:

```bash
# nano-bench
bun `npx nano-bench --self` benchmark.js
deno run -A `npx nano-bench --self` benchmark.js

# nano-watch
bun `npx nano-watch --self` benchmark.js methodName
deno run -A `npx nano-watch --self` benchmark.js methodName
```

For Deno, `--allow-read` is required and `--allow-hrtime` is recommended. Use `-A` for convenience in safe environments.

---

## Statistical methods

### Bootstrap median, CI, and spread

`bootstrapSummary` resamples the timing data with replacement `--bootstrap` times and reports three things. The **median** is the mean of the resampled medians. The **CI** (`ciLo`, `ciHi`) is the bootstrap percentile confidence interval of the median: the α/2 and 1−α/2 percentiles of those resampled medians; it narrows roughly with the square root of the sample count, and `nano-bench-io --stable` stops on its width. The **spread** (`lo`, `hi`) is the mean across resamples of the α/2 and 1−α/2 quantiles of the samples: the range most runs fall in, which does not narrow with more samples. The CI reuses the medians already drawn, so adding it left the seeded median and spread unchanged. The RNG is `mulberry32` seeded by `--seed` (or an auto-recorded seed), with a distinct per-series stream, so all three are reproducible exactly on recompute. Before the bootstrap completes, an exact order-statistic estimate of the median and spread is shown and then overwritten.

### Mann-Whitney U test

Nonparametric two-sample test used when comparing exactly 2 functions; normal approximation, two-sided, tie-corrected. Tests whether the two timing distributions are significantly different at the given `--alpha` level. Does not assume a normal distribution. A single comparison, so no multiplicity correction applies. Reports the effect size alongside: Vargha-Delaney A12 = U₁/(n₁·n₂) (probability a random run of one function exceeds a random run of the other, ties half-counted — derived from the same rank sums) and Cliff's δ = 2·A12 − 1, labeled negligible/small/medium/large per Romano et al. thresholds (0.147/0.33/0.474). Significance says a difference exists; the effect size says how much.

### Kruskal-Wallis H test + Conover-Iman post-hoc

Nonparametric k-sample test used when comparing 3+ functions. The omnibus uses a beta approximation for the null distribution of H. If the omnibus is significant, the **Conover-Iman** pairwise post-hoc (Fisher's LSD on the shared ranks, with the Student t critical value approximated by z for large df) identifies which specific pairs differ.

### Multiple-comparison correction

The k(k−1)/2 Conover-Iman pairwise comparisons within one omnibus inflate the family-wise error rate. `--correction` controls it, acting on the per-comparison critical value (`zPpf(1 − α/2)`):

- `holm` (default) — Holm step-down: sort the comparisons by strength and test against progressively relaxed thresholds, stopping at the first failure. Same FWER guarantee as Bonferroni but uniformly more powerful, so it is the default.
- `bonferroni` — single-step; every comparison tested at α/m. More conservative; kept for its familiarity.
- `none` — uncorrected (reproduces the earlier, pre-correction post-hoc behaviour).

The correction touches only the significance path, not the bootstrap CI's α (a CI is one interval, not a family). The 2-series Mann-Whitney case and separate paired-by-name compare blocks are single comparisons (m = 1, uncorrected).

### Distribution histograms

`--histogram` renders each function's sample distribution as an inline terminal chart, on a shared range/bin set so series are comparable. It surfaces multimodality, skew, and outlier tails (GC pauses, JIT warmup) that a single median+CI line cannot show. Bin count is automatic (scaled to the sample count, capped to the terminal), overridable with `--bins`; orientation is `columns` (vertical ridgeline) or `bars` (horizontal). Median (▾) and mean (▿) markers and a multimodality nudge annotate each chart.

### Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

Two-sample distribution comparison test. Available in the library API (`src/significance/kstest.js`), not wired into the CLI.

### Online/streaming algorithms

Used by nano-watch for indefinite monitoring with constant memory:

- **StatCounter** — Welford's online algorithm for streaming mean, variance (M2), skewness (M3), and kurtosis (M4). Numerically stable single-pass computation.
- **MedianCounter** — approximate streaming median using a hierarchical median-of-three structure. Provides O(1) memory approximate median without storing all values.

---

## User Timing API integration

The `nano-bench` CLI accepts `-o` / `--observe`. When set, calibration and sampling phases emit `performance.mark` and `performance.measure` entries to the standard performance timeline. Observers can subscribe via `PerformanceObserver`; the entries are also visible in DevTools / `node --inspect` traces.

Mark and measure names follow the convention `nano-bench/<label>/<phase>`:

- Start mark: `nano-bench/<label>/<phase>:start`
- Measure: `nano-bench/<label>/<phase>` (with the start mark as its start)

Phases are:

- `find-level` — calibration (auto-discovery of batch size).
- `rounds` — interleaved sample collection (the default); its label is `all`, since a round covers every function (`nano-bench/all/rounds`).
- `series` — sequential sample collection (`--order sequential`).
- `series-par` — parallel sample collection (when `--parallel` is set).

The CLI uses each function's exported name as the label, so multiple benchmarks in one run produce distinct entries (e.g., `nano-bench/strings/find-level`, `nano-bench/backticks/series`, etc.).

### Consumer example

```js
import {PerformanceObserver} from 'node:perf_hooks';

const obs = new PerformanceObserver(list => {
  for (const e of list.getEntries()) {
    console.log(`${e.name}: ${e.duration.toFixed(2)} ms`);
  }
});
obs.observe({entryTypes: ['measure']});
```

### Library API

The orchestrating runner functions accept an `observe` option (`boolean | string`):

- `false` / `undefined` — no instrumentation (default).
- `true` — emit marks with the default label `"default"`.
- string — emit marks with the given label.

The option is supported by `findLevel`, `benchmarkSeries`, `benchmarkSeriesPar`, `benchmarkRounds`, `measure`, and `measurePar`. `measure` / `measurePar` thread it through to the inner `findLevel` and `benchmarkSeries` / `benchmarkSeriesPar` calls so a single `observe` argument produces both calibration and sample-collection entries.

```js
import {measure} from 'nano-benchmark/bench/runner.js';

const fn = n => { let s = 0; for (let i = 0; i < n; ++i) s += i; };
const stats = await measure(fn, {nSeries: 50, observe: 'sum-loop'});
```

### Cost

Marks have a small fixed cost per phase (one `performance.mark` + one `performance.measure` per phase boundary, not per sample). Per-sample timing remains pure `performance.now()` deltas, so observe-mode does not measurably affect benchmark accuracy. The default is off purely to keep the perf timeline buffer empty for users who don't need the integration.

The `nano-watch` CLI deliberately does **not** expose `--observe` because its sample loop is unbounded by default; library users who want to instrument continuous monitoring should manage their own buffer (e.g., `performance.clearMarks()` periodically) via the library API.
